about: Zipacna, safe in the second pit he has dug at the side, calls up to the four hundred boys to come and take away the earth, for he has gone far down, and he can hear them. They drag up their great tree and let it fall into the pit, telling one another to keep quiet and listen for his cry; he cries out once, and they rejoice that he is dead and plan three days of drinking at the dedication of their house, once the ants have come for the body. Zipacna hears them. He cuts off his hair and gnaws off his nails and gives them to the ants, and when the boys see the ants carrying hair and nails they are sure he is dead. On the third day, when they are all drunk, he brings their house down on their heads, and not one of them is saved; it is said that they became the stars called Motz, the Pleiades. Then a new section: Hunahpu and Xbalanque, grieved by the death of the four hundred, make a false crab, with a shell of stone, and set it in a cave under the mountain Meauan. They meet Zipacna by the river, hungry for two days for want of fish and crabs, and tell him of a great crab in the ravine that bit them when they went in face down. He begs them to show him the way, and they tell him that it would be well for him to go in on his back.

sentences.t: Ma cu are cu cot vxe hul ri vmoquiquil; xa vhul cu coto colbal rib.
sentences.l: Not then this he-digs its-base pit the his-burial(?); only his-pit he-digs, saving himself.
sentences.i: It was not the bottom of the pit, the one meant for his burial, that he was digging; the pit he was digging was his own, to save himself.
sentences.n: Ma … xa 'not … only' sets the two halves against each other: not the boys' pit, but his own. cu cot 'he digs': c- (ongoing) + v- 'he' (written together as cu) + cot 'dig', the verb of the last part (Ca coto, xucot), respelled as written in the toggle. vxe hul 'the base of the pit'. vmoquiquil is clear in the image; Brasseur's OCR has a garbled ri u iki and his French 'for a tomb'. It may come from muc 'bury', 'his burial', but the manuscript has o, not u, and the word is printed as read and respelled letter for letter; the sense is inferred. colbal rib 'a saving of himself': col 'save' + -bal, as vcolbal rib in the last part.

sentences.t: Cate cut ta xziquin vloc ri Zipacna, colon chu ca chiri pa hul, ta xziquin vloc:
sentences.l: Then then when called hither the Zipacna, safe at-its second(?) there in pit, when he-called hither:
sentences.i: Then Zipacna called up, safe there in the second pit; he called up:
sentences.n: xziquin vloc 'he called hither', up to the boys: ziquin 'call, shout', as in the last part (toggle sik'in). colon 'safe, freed', taken from col 'save'; inferred. chu ca: a blot covers the third letter in the manuscript (chu?a), and Brasseur's OCR has chu ca (its first word garbled), which is followed; ca is taken as cab 'second' without its b, as vca hul 'a second pit' in the last part, so 'in the second (pit)', with Brasseur's French ('in the other hole'); inferred. colon is clear in the image.

sentences.t: “Quix petoc, chul icama vleu, rachac hul mi xcototahic.
sentences.l: “You(pl.)-come, come-here you(pl.)-take earth, its-refuse(?) pit just-now it-was-dug.
sentences.i: “Come, come and take away the earth, the rubble of the pit that has been dug.
sentences.n: Quix petoc 'come, you (pl.)': c- + ix 'you (pl.)' + pet 'come' + -oc. chul 'come here', ch- (command) + ul 'arrive here', the 'you (pl.)' of quix carried over; inferred (Brasseur ch'ul). icama 'you (pl.) take': i- + cama, the 'take' of the last part (inferred). rachac 'its refuse' is a guess after Brasseur ('the debris'); achac is a word for dung, refuse. mi xcototahic 'that has just been dug': x- + cot 'dig' + -o- + -tah (passive) + -ic.

sentences.t: Quiꜩih nah mi xcah vvmal.
sentences.l: Truly far just-now it-went-down by-me.
sentences.i: Truly, I have gone far down.
sentences.n: xcah 'went down', the verb qaj of the last part. vvmal 'by me': v- 'my' + vmal, the umal of rumal 'by it'. The line breaks v-|vmal, so the manuscript has vvmal, printed as written (Brasseur vumal; avmal 'by you' in the last part). Word for word 'truly far it has gone down by me'.

sentences.t: Mapa qui ta nu ziquibal lo?
sentences.l: Not(?) you(pl.)-hear my-calling perhaps?
sentences.i: Do you not hear me calling?
sentences.n: Mapa: ma 'not' + pa, the question word, 'is it not that…?'. qui ta 'you (pl.) hear': c- (ongoing) + i- 'you (pl.)' + ta 'hear'; the manuscript runs quita together. nu ziquibal 'my calling': ziquin 'call' + -ibal. lo 'perhaps' softens the question.

sentences.t: Are curi iziquibal xa vbi ca xohanic, queheri hun elebal, caib elebal; ix ꜭo vi ca nu tao,” xꜭha vla ri Zipacna pa vhul.
sentences.l: This then your(pl.)-calling, only its-name(?) ca xohanic(?), like one echo(?), two echoes(?); you there-are there, I-hear,” he-said hither the Zipacna in his-pit.
sentences.i: As for your calling, only its sound is echoed, like one echo, two echoes; you are there, I can hear you,” Zipacna called up from his pit.
sentences.n: iziquibal 'your (pl.) calling', i- + ziquibal. xa vbi ca xohanic is not clear: vbi 'its name' is taken as 'the mere sound of it', and xohanic is not otherwise known; the rendering follows Brasseur ('the sound of it is echoed'), a guess. elebal: el 'go out' + -ebal, 'a going out', taken with Brasseur as an echo; hun elebal, caib elebal 'one echo, two echoes' is a couplet. ix ꜭo vi 'you are there'. ca nu tao 'I hear (it)': c- + nu- 'I' + ta 'hear' + -o. pa vhul 'in his pit', his own.

sentences.t: Chiri cut maꜩal chi vi vloc ca ziquiah chi vla pa hul.
sentences.l: There then maꜩal(?) again there hither he-calls again hither in pit.
sentences.i: There he was, sheltering, and from there he kept calling up out of the pit.
sentences.n: maꜩal: the first letter of its line has the t-stroke of the tz ligature; Brasseur's OCR is garbled here, and the word is not otherwise known. Brasseur's French ('the pit where he had sheltered') suggests 'sheltered', a guess. ca ziquiah 'he calls': a heavy stroke over the z makes it look like the ligature, but it is read plain z with Brasseur (ca ziquiyah) and the verb ziquin of the lines before. chi, twice, is taken as chic 'again' written without its c (no c follows to share it, unlike chi cut 'again then'); it may be the preposition chi; inferred.

sentences.t: Are cut ca hurux vloc ri qui nima che rumal ꜭaholab; cate puch xquitarih cahoc ri che pa hul.
sentences.l: This then is-dragged(?) hither the their great tree by boys; then also they-let-fall(?) down the tree in pit.
sentences.i: Then the boys dragged up their great tree, and let the tree fall down into the pit.
sentences.n: ca hurux 'it is dragged': hur 'drag' (as in the last part) + -x, a passive; inferred. The manuscript has cahu-|ruxvloc, divided here; Brasseur's OCR has a garbled ca harax(?) uloc, and the image is followed. xquitarih 'they let fall': x- + qui- 'they' + tarih, inferred as in the last part (Brasseur 'they threw'). cahoc 'downward' (qaj 'go down' + -oc).

sentences.t: “Ma ꜭo ma ꜭhauic; chi ca tana ta chu racuh vchi, ta camoc,” xecha chi quibil quib.
sentences.l: “Not there-is not speaking; that we tana(?) when he-scrapes(?) his-mouth, when he-dies,” they-said among themselves.
sentences.i: “Let no one speak; let us listen for him to cry out, and to die,” they said to one another.
sentences.n: Ma ꜭo ma ꜭhauic 'there is not, not speaking', that is, let no one speak. chi ca tana: tana is not known (it stood beside chaquimah in the last part); Brasseur takes the clause as 'let us wait', and 'listen' is a guess. chu racuh vchi 'he scrapes his mouth', taken as 'he cries out', as in the last part (inferred). camoc 'let him die': cam 'die' + -oc. xecha: the verb of speaking is written here with plain ch, not ꜭh, and printed as written.

sentences.t: Xa que hazlahic, xa pu chi maꜩalah qui vach chi qui huhunal, ta xquitarih cahoc ri che.
sentences.l: Only they whispered(?), only also (chi) maꜩalah(?) their faces to their each-one, when they-let-fall down the tree.
sentences.i: They only whispered, and only glanced at one another, each at each, as they let the tree fall.
sentences.n: que hazlahic 'they whispered(?)': que is c- (ongoing) + e 'they'; hazlahic is not otherwise known, and 'whisper' follows Brasseur ('speaking in secret'). maꜩalah qui vach chi qui huhunal 'they maꜩalah their faces, each to each': Brasseur 'looking at one another'; maꜩalah may share its root with maꜩal above; both inferred. The manuscript has the tz ligature here.

sentences.t: Are cu xꜭha cut ta xuracuh vchi, xa hupah chic xziquinic, ta xcah apanoc ri che.
sentences.l: This then he-said then when he-scraped(?) his-mouth, only once again he-called, when went-down away the tree.
sentences.i: Then he spoke, crying out; he called out only once more, as the tree went down.
sentences.n: xuracuh vchi 'he cried out': x- + v- 'he' + racuh, the phrase of the boys' speech above. hupah 'once': hu(n) 'one' + pah, inferred. xziquinic 'he called': x- + ziquin + -ic. apanoc 'away, over there' (apan 'go there' + -oc).

sentences.t: “Oca mi xuꜩinic qui vꜩ mi xca bano chire! Mi xcamic.
sentences.l: “Oca(?) just-now it-succeeded how good just-now we did to-him! Just-now he-died.
sentences.i: “Ah, it has come right — how well we have dealt with him! He is dead.
sentences.n: Oca is taken as a cry of joy, after Brasseur ('Oh!'); a guess. mi 'just now' marks what has just happened: mi xuꜩinic 'it has come right', x- + vꜩin 'be finished, come right' (vꜩ 'good' + -in; chuꜩinoc 'let it be finished' in the last part) + -ic. qui vꜩ 'how good': qui is taken as a word of degree before vꜩ 'good'; inferred. mi xca bano chire 'what we have done to him': x- + ca- 'we' + bano. Mi xcamic 'he has died'.

sentences.t: Atalabe chi taquen chu bano, chu chacuh, ta chuxoc!
sentences.l: Atalabe(?) that he-keeps-on(?) he-does-it, he-works-it, then let-it-be!
sentences.i: If he had kept on with what he was doing, with what he was working at, it would have been all over!
sentences.n: Atalabe is not otherwise known; Brasseur's French ('if by ill luck he had continued the work') takes it as 'if, by mischance', and the sentence is rendered after him, inferred. taquen 'keep on, follow' (inferred, after Brasseur); the same letters begin taquentah in the third part, taken there as 'be sent'. chu bano, chu chacuh 'he do it, he work it': a couplet; chacuh from chac 'work'. ta chuxoc 'then let it be (so)': the 'end of us' is not in the words, which leave it unsaid.

sentences.t: Vnabe la xucoh vla rib cuꜭ, chi caxol puch la, oh omuch ꜭaholab.”
sentences.l: His-first la he-put hither himself with-us, at our-midst also la, we four-hundred boys.”
sentences.i: He was the first to put himself among us, into our very midst, we the four hundred boys.”
sentences.n: Vnabe 'his first', 'he was the first'. la is the particle that appeared in the third, fifth and last parts; Brasseur calls it a particle of elegance, and here it is left untranslated. xucoh … rib 'he put himself': x- + v- + coh 'put'. cuꜭ 'with us' (q- 'our' + uꜭ), the q-shaped letter read ꜭ with Brasseur. caxol 'our midst': ca- 'our' + xol 'between'.

sentences.t: Xeꜭha cut, que quicot chic: “Ꜭo ri vbanic ca qui oxih, que ecouic oxih puch chi cucah lacabebal ca cabal la, oh omuch chi ꜭaholab,” xeꜭha.
sentences.l: They-said then, they rejoicing now: “There-is the its-making our drink three-days(?), they-pass(?) three(?) also that we-drink(?) dedication(?) our house la, we four-hundred (chi) boys,” they-said.
sentences.i: So they said, rejoicing now: “Now our drink is to be made, for three days, and three more days are to pass in drinking at the dedication of our house, we the four hundred boys,” they said.
sentences.n: que quicot chic 'rejoicing now': que 'they (ongoing)' + quicot 'rejoice', the verb of the first part. qui is taken with Brasseur as the fermented drink (his quiy, which he says is the general word for such drinks); oxih as ox 'three' + ꜫih 'day', 'three days', also after his note; both inferred, and the toggle respells the letters. que ecouic: the manuscript has que (blotted) and then e, a letter struck through and ecouic; the struck letter is left out. ecouic is taken as the verb of icouic 'pass' (the last part), Brasseur eqouic; inferred and respelled as written. cucah 'we drink': c- for q- 'we' (before a vowel) + uk' 'drink' + -ah (Brasseur k'uqah, his q = ꜭ; French 'to drink'); the verb is certain, so the toggle restores the ejective (quk'aj), here and in the next line. lacabebal 'dedication' follows Brasseur ('the founding of our houses'); not otherwise known.

sentences.t: “Chuvec cut chi quilo; cabih puch chi quilo, mapa chi pe zanic pu vleu ta chuinoc, ta ꜫeyoc;
sentences.l: “Tomorrow then that we-see; day-after-tomorrow also that we-see, whether that come ants pu(?) earth when it-stinks(?), when ꜫeyoc(?);
sentences.i: “Tomorrow we shall see, and the day after we shall see, whether the ants come into the earth when he stinks, when he rots;
sentences.n: A couplet: chuvec 'tomorrow', cabih 'the day after tomorrow'. chi quilo 'we shall see': q- 'we' (written c/qu before a vowel) + il 'see' + -o. mapa 'whether perhaps'. zanic 'ants'. pu vleu: pu is not clear ('also'?, or 'in'?), and 'into the earth' is a guess. chuinoc 'when it stinks': chu 'stink' + -in + -oc, inferred. ꜫeyoc: Ximénez writes a q-shaped letter + u where Brasseur has g (gey-oc), so it is read ꜫ and the u dropped; the word is not otherwise known, and 'rots' is a guess made from the couplet.

sentences.t: cate cut cul chi ca ꜭux ta cucah ri ca qui,” xeꜭha cut.
sentences.l: then then it-comes (chi) our-heart when we-drink(?) the our drink,” they-said then.
sentences.i: then our hearts will be at ease, as we drink our drink,” they said.
sentences.n: cul chi ca ꜭux 'our heart comes (to rest)': cul 'it comes' (c- + ul); 'at ease' follows Brasseur ('our heart will rest'), inferred. ca ꜭux 'our heart': the manuscript has chicagux, a q-shaped letter read ꜭ with Brasseur (his q). cucah ri ca qui 'we drink our drink', as above.

sentences.t: Cu ta cu vloc ri Zipacna chiri pa hul, ta xquibih ꜭaholab ri.
sentences.l: He-hears then hither the Zipacna there in pit, when they-said boys this.
sentences.i: Zipacna, there in the pit, heard what the boys said.
sentences.n: Cu ta 'he hears': c- + v- 'he' (written cu) + ta 'hear'; the second cu is the particle 'then'. vloc 'hither': the words came down to him. xquibih 'they said': x- + qui- + bih 'say'.

sentences.t: Ca chu cabih puch, ta xtubuquih zanic, que binouic, que buchuvic, ta xeculun xe che.
sentences.l: Ca at-its day-after-tomorrow also, when swarmed(?) ants, they walking, they crowding(?), when they-gathered(?) root tree.
sentences.i: And on the second day the ants came swarming, going along, crowding together, and gathered under the tree.
sentences.n: Ca chu cabih 'on the second day': the image has ca, Brasseur Cu, and the image is printed. xtubuquih 'swarmed' is inferred from Brasseur ('arrived all at once'). que binouic, que buchuvic 'they walking, they crowding': a couplet; bin 'walk' + -ou- + -ic; buchuvic is inferred ('in a mass', Brasseur). xeculun 'they gathered' is inferred, after Brasseur ('to gather under the tree'). xe che 'at the foot of the tree'.

sentences.t: Humah qui cayeloon iz, qui cayeloon puch rixcac Zipacna.
sentences.l: Some their carrying(?) hair, their carrying(?) also his-nails Zipacna.
sentences.i: Some were carrying hair, and some were carrying Zipacna's nails.
sentences.n: A couplet. Humah 'some' (hu- 'one' + mah), inferred. qui cayeloon 'they carrying', inferred after Brasseur ('some carried hair'); the double o is the manuscript's. iz 'hair', after Brasseur (rizmal 'his hair' below). rixcac 'his nails': r- + ixcac 'fingernail' (modern ixk'aq). Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur has g (r'ixgag); the word is certain, so the toggle gives the modern rixk'aq, here and below, as with xecabar and chacab in this part.

sentences.t: Ta xquil curi ꜭaholab: “Mi pa xuꜩin ri ꜭaxtoꜭ?
sentences.l: Then they-saw then boys: “Just-now (pa) it-is-finished the demon?
sentences.i: When the boys saw it: “Is the demon finished, then?
sentences.n: xquil 'they saw': x- + qui- + il, without the -o. Mi pa xuꜩin 'has he finished?': pa makes it a question, and xuꜩin 'it has come to an end' is the verb of xuꜩinic above. ꜭaxtoꜭ 'demon', the word Vucub Caquix used of Hunahpu and Xbalanque in the fifth part; here the boys' word for Zipacna.

sentences.t: Chi vila na zanic mi xeculun vloc, mi xetubuquih vloc, humah iz qui caien, ꜭo rixcac; ri chila na mi xca bano,” ca xeꜭha chi quibil quib.
sentences.l: See (you-pl.) now ants just-now they-gathered hither, just-now they-swarmed hither, some hair they-carry(?), there-are his-nails; the there now just-now we did,” ca they-said among themselves.
sentences.i: “Look at the ants: they have gathered here, they have come swarming here, some carrying hair, and there are his nails; that is what we did there,” they said to one another.
sentences.n: Chi vila 'look, you (pl.)': ch- (command) + iv- 'you (pl.)' (i- before a vowel) + il 'see' + -a, as Brasseur writes it (ch'yv 'ila); the manuscript runs chivila together. mi xeculun, mi xetubuquih: a couplet. qui caien 'they carry', taken as a short form of cayeloon above; inferred. ri chila na mi xca bano 'that is what we have done there'. ca xeꜭha: ca is not clear (Brasseur Ca x-e cha); left unrendered.

sentences.t: Are curi Zipacna xa vi ꜭazlic; xuꜫat vloc rizmal v vi, xa pu cu qux vloc rixcac chire, cu ya vla chiquech ri zanic.
sentences.l: This then Zipacna only (vi) alive; he-cut hither his-hair its head, only also he gnawed(?) hither his-nails at-his-teeth(?), he gives hither to-them the ants.
sentences.i: But Zipacna was alive. He had cut the hair from his head, and gnawed off his nails with his teeth, and given them to the ants.
sentences.n: xa vi ꜭazlic 'still alive': ꜭazlic 'living', the root of ꜭazlem 'life'. xuꜫat 'he cut': the letter after xu looks like t in the image (its final t retouched); it is taken as ꜫ with Brasseur (x-u gat), the hand being ambiguous, a doubtful reading; the verb is q'at 'cut' as in the last part. v vi 'its head' (vi 'head', not vi 'there'). cu qux: the letter is q-shaped where Brasseur has plain c (c'u cux), and it is printed qu; his note gives cuz 'saw', and 'gnawed' is inferred; the toggle respells the letters. chire 'at his teeth' is inferred (chi + r- 'his' + e 'tooth', as re 'his teeth' in the last part; Brasseur 'with his teeth'). cu ya 'he gives'.

sentences.t: Quehe curi xcamic xquinao omuch ꜭaholab.
sentences.l: Thus then he-died they-felt four-hundred boys.
sentences.i: So the four hundred boys thought that he was dead.
sentences.n: xquinao 'they felt, they thought': x- + qui- + nao, the verb of xca nao in the fourth part and xunao in the last. The thing thought (xcamic 'he died') stands before the verb.

sentences.t: Cate cut xticar qui qui chi roxih, ta xecabar puch conohel ꜭaholab.
sentences.l: Then then began their drink on its-third, when they-got-drunk also all boys.
sentences.i: Then, on the third day, their drinking began, and all the boys got drunk.
sentences.n: xticar 'it began': x- + ticar 'begin' (as xticaric in the last part). Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur has q (x-tiqar), and it is printed as written. qui qui 'their drink': the manuscript breaks q-|ui qui, read qui qui (Brasseur qui quiy). roxih 'its third (day)': r- + oxih, as above. xecabar 'they got drunk': Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur has g (that is ꜫ), and the word is the certain q'ab'ar 'be drunk', so the toggle restores the ejective, here and in cabarinac.

sentences.t: E ca cabarinac chic conohel omuch ꜭaholab, mahabi ca qui na chic.
sentences.l: They ca drunk now all four-hundred boys, there-was-not ca their feeling(?) now.
sentences.i: All four hundred boys were drunk now, and had no sense left in them.
sentences.n: E ca cabarinac: the image has eca, Brasseur E cu; the image is printed. cabarinac 'drunk': -inac is the perfect participle, 'having got drunk'. ca is not clear in either place (perhaps cu 'then'). qui na 'their feeling': na 'feel', as in xquinao; mahabi … chic 'no longer'; inferred.

sentences.t: Cate puch xulix ri cabal pa qui vi rumal ri Zipacna; xequiz chayatahic conohel.
sentences.l: Then also was-brought-down the house on their heads by the Zipacna; they-finished being-struck-down(?) all.
sentences.i: Then Zipacna brought the house down on their heads, and they were all struck down, to the last.
sentences.n: xulix 'it was brought down': x- + ul + -ix (passive), inferred (Brasseur 'overturned'). pa qui vi 'on their heads': vi 'head'. xequiz 'they finished': x- + e 'they' + quiz 'end, be finished', the k'is of the last part; the q-shaped letter is printed qu as there. chayatahic 'being struck down': chay 'strike' + -atah (passive) + -ic, inferred.

sentences.t: Mahabi chic hun, caib xcolotah chiquech ri omuch chi ꜭaholab; xecamizaxic rumal Zipacna, vꜭahol ri Vucub Caquix.
sentences.l: There-was-not now one, two was-saved from-them the four-hundred (chi) boys; they-were-killed by Zipacna, his-son the Vucub Caquix.
sentences.i: Not one, not two of the four hundred boys was saved; they were killed by Zipacna, the son of Vucub Caquix.
sentences.n: Mahabi chic hun, caib 'not one, two', not even one or two. xcolotah 'was saved', as in the last part. chiquech 'from among them' (chi + quech). xecamizaxic 'they were killed': x- + e + camiz 'kill' + -ax- (passive) + -ic.

sentences.t: Quehe cut qui camic omuch ꜭaholab ri; xꜭha chi cut, are ri xeoc chi chumilal, ri Moꜩ vbi cumal; ve cut xa zacbal ꜩih lo.
sentences.l: Thus then their death four-hundred boys this; it-is-said also then, this that they-entered into starriness, the Moꜩ its-name by-them; if then only zacbal(?) word perhaps.
sentences.i: Such was the death of the four hundred boys; and it is said too that they went into the stars, into the cluster called Motz because of them — though that may be only a tale.
sentences.n: xꜭha chi cut 'it is said also': chi is chic, its c shared with cut, and the toggle shows chik, as in the earlier parts. xeoc chi chumilal 'they entered into starhood': x- + e + oc 'enter' + chi + chumil 'star' (toggle ch'umil, as in the fourth part) + -al. Moꜩ is the K'iche' name of the Pleiades, the small cluster of stars; Brasseur gives motz 'group, heap' as its meaning. vbi cumal 'its name by them' may mean that the stars are called after the boys, or that people call them so. ve cut xa zacbal ꜩih lo 'if, though, it is only a zacbal word': zacbal is not otherwise known (perhaps from zac 'white, clear'), and 'a tale' follows Brasseur ('a fiction'); with Brasseur's zakbal (his k = q) and zac, the toggle gives saqb'al.

sentences.t: Are chi cut chi ca biyh vchacatahic chic Zipacna rumal ri e caib ꜭaholab, Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: This now then that we-tell his-being-brought-low again Zipacna by the (e) two boys, Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: Now we shall tell how Zipacna in his turn was brought low by the two boys, Hunahpu and Xbalanque.
sentences.n: Are chi cut 'now then': chi is chic, its c shared with cut (Brasseur chicut). chi ca biyh 'we shall tell': ca- 'we' + biyh 'say, tell', the byih of xchicabyih in the earlier parts, here with its letters in another order. vchacatahic 'his being brought low', the word used of his father in the fifth part. e 'they', the plural before caib ꜭaholab.

sentences.t: Are chic vchacatahic, vcamic Zipacna, ta xchac chic cumal ri e caib ꜭaholab, Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: This now his-being-brought-low, his-death Zipacna, when he-was-beaten again by-them the (e) two boys, Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: Here is the overthrow and the death of Zipacna, when he was beaten in his turn by the two boys, Hunahpu and Xbalanque.
sentences.n: Here Ximénez starts a new section, with a large A. vchacatahic, vcamic 'his overthrow, his death': a couplet. xchac 'he was beaten', taken with chac 'win, overcome', the root of vchacatahic; inferred. cumal 'by them'.

sentences.t: Are chic vyoc qui ꜭux caholab ri omuch chi ꜭaholab xecamic rumal Zipacna.
sentences.l: This now its-wounding(?) their heart boys, the four-hundred (chi) boys they-died by Zipacna.
sentences.i: What wounded the boys' hearts was that the four hundred boys had been killed by Zipacna.
sentences.n: vyoc qui ꜭux 'the wounding of their heart' follows Brasseur ('what wounded the heart'); vyoc is not otherwise known. qui ꜭux: the manuscript has quiqux, a q-shaped letter read ꜭ with Brasseur. caholab: the image has plain c here, where every other instance of the word has ꜭ; it is printed as written, and since the word is certain the toggle shows k'ajolab'. The boys whose hearts are wounded are taken, with Brasseur, to be Hunahpu and Xbalanque.

sentences.t: Xa car, xa tap chuꜩucuh chi taca, xere chirechaah hutaꜫih;
sentences.l: Only fish, only crab he-sought at taca(?), only-this to-his-food every-day;
sentences.i: Fish and crabs alone he would look for along the waters; that alone was his food each day;
sentences.n: Zipacna is the subject. xa car, xa tap 'only fish, only crab', a couplet. chuꜩucuh 'he would seek': ch- + v- 'he' + ꜩucuh 'look for' (modern tzukuj), here of what he did by habit; inferred. Brasseur prints tzukuh (his k is q) and reads 'he fed', but the sense 'seek' fits ca nu ꜩucuh 'I am looking for' below (Brasseur 'I seek'). This is not the tzuq 'feed, sustain' of ꜩucul and the last part's ꜩucubei, though the letters are close. chi taca: Brasseur divides chi tak a 'by the rivers'; it is kept undivided as written, and 'along the waters' is inferred; with his division the toggle shows taqa, taq being the plural word (tac in unit 36). chirechaah 'to be his food', chi + r- + echa + -ah. hutaꜫih 'every day': the manuscript has hutaquih, a q-shaped letter + u where Brasseur has g, read ꜫ.

sentences.t: pa ꜫih chi vacatic ta chuꜩucuh recha; chacab cut chi recah huyub.
sentences.l: in day that he-wanders(?) when he-seeks his-food; at-night then that he-carries-on-back mountain.
sentences.i: by day he went about looking for his food, and by night he carried mountains on his back.
sentences.n: A couplet of day and night. pa ꜫih 'by day': the manuscript has quih, read ꜫih as above. vacatic 'wandering' is inferred from Brasseur ('he went about'). chacab 'at night': chi + acab, taken as aꜫab 'night'; Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur has g (ch'agab), and the word is certain, so the toggle shows chaq'ab'. recah 'he carries it on his back': r- + ecah, the carrying with a strap (Brasseur 'he loaded the mountains on his shoulders').

sentences.t: Cate cut vhalvachixic hun nima tap cumal Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: Then then its-being-given-a-changed-face one great crab by-them Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: Then Hunahpu and Xbalanque made a false likeness of a great crab.
sentences.n: vhalvachixic: hal 'change' + vach 'face' + -ix- (passive) + -ic, 'the making of a changed face', a likeness, a counterfeit (Brasseur 'imitated'); inferred.

sentences.t: Are cut xquicoh ri vvach ec, ri mac ec ꜭo pa tac quechelah.
sentences.l: This then they-put the its-face(?) ec(?), the mac(?) ec(?) there-is in (tac) forests.
sentences.i: For its head they used ec, the ec that grows all through the forests.
sentences.n: xquicoh 'they put, used': x- + qui- + coh 'put'. ec is a plant: Brasseur says a wild plant with large leaves, used to deck triumphal arches; which plant is not known. vvach 'its face' is taken with Brasseur as the crab's head; inferred. mac is not otherwise known. pa tac quechelah 'in the forests': tac makes the plural. In quechelah the letter is q-shaped where Brasseur has q, printed qu as in the earlier parts.

sentences.t: Are vxul tap xuxic, pahac chi cut vcoc ꜫab; xquicoho zelabah curi vva rachac tap rihouohic.
sentences.l: This its-xul(?) crab became, pahac(?) (chi) then its-coc(?) hand; they-put zelabah(?) then its-face its-achac(?) crab rihouohic(?).
sentences.i: That became the crab's legs, and pahac its small legs; and they put on a shell of stone for the crab's face and its back.
sentences.n: Much here is guessed. vxul tap 'the crab's xul': Brasseur 'the great legs' (les grandes pattes), inferred. pahac: Brasseur could not find the word and names elsewhere paak, a kind of fruit tree; what it is here is not known. pahac chi cut: chi is chic, its c shared with cut (Brasseur chicut). vcoc ꜫab: Brasseur 'the small legs'; vcoc is the word of the last part, and coc may be 'shell' (in the next sentence Brasseur reads it 'turtle'); a guess. ꜫab 'hand': the tresillo in the manuscript. zelabah is taken as a flat stone (abah 'stone'; Brasseur 'a shell of stone'). vva 'its face', as in the fourth part. rachac and rihouohic are not clear (rih 'its back'?); the last clause follows Brasseur in outline only.

sentences.t: Cate cut ta xquicoh vcoc chuxe pec, chuxe nima huyub; Meauan vbi huyub, xchacatah vi.
sentences.l: Then then when they-put its-coc(?) at-foot cave, at-foot great mountain; Meauan its-name mountain, he-was-brought-low there.
sentences.i: Then they set it at the foot of a cave, at the foot of a great mountain; Meauan is the name of the mountain where he was overcome.
sentences.n: chuxe pec, chuxe nima huyub 'at the foot of a cave, at the foot of a great mountain': a couplet. vcoc as above, here 'its shell, the crab' (Brasseur 'this kind of turtle'); inferred. Meauan is the mountain's name; its meaning is not known. xchacatah vi 'where he was overcome': the passive of vchacatahic, told ahead of the event.

sentences.t: Cate cut ta xepe ri ꜭaholab, xquicu ri Zipacna chi ya.
sentences.l: Then then when they-came the boys, they-met the Zipacna at river.
sentences.i: Then the boys came along and met Zipacna by the river.
sentences.n: xepe 'they came': x- + e + pe. xquicu 'they met': x- + qui- + cu, inferred (Brasseur 'went to meet'). ya 'river, water', after Brasseur ('by the river'); the toggle respells the letters.

sentences.t: “Apa cat be vi, at ꜭahol?” xchax curi Zipacna.
sentences.l: “Where you go there, you boy?” was-told then Zipacna.
sentences.i: “Where are you going, boy?” they asked Zipacna.
sentences.n: Apa … vi 'where'. cat be 'you are going': c- + at 'you (one)' + be 'go'. xchax 'he was told': x- + cha 'say' + -x (passive); the image has plain ch, printed as written (Brasseur x-chax). The toggle shows ch' in the passive of this verb, as xuchaxic in the last part.

sentences.t: “Mahabi quin be vi; xa vecha ca nu ꜩucuh, ix ꜭaholab,” xꜭha curi Zipacna.
sentences.l: “There-is-not I-go there; only my-food I-seek, you boys,” he-said then Zipacna.
sentences.i: “I am going nowhere; I am only looking for my food, boys,” said Zipacna.
sentences.n: Mahabi quin be vi 'nowhere am I going': quin 'I (ongoing)', c- + in. A small k-like mark above the space between Mahabi and quin is not a letter of the text and is not printed. vecha 'my food': v- 'my' + echa. ca nu ꜩucuh 'I am looking for': c- + nu- 'I' + ꜩucuh.

sentences.t: “Naquipa avecha?” “Xa car, xa tap; xma ꜭo chi vi ca nu rico.
sentences.l: “What your-food?” “Only fish, only crab; not there-is (chi) there I-find.
sentences.i: “What is your food?” “Only fish, only crabs; and there are none for me to find.
sentences.n: avecha 'your food': av- (a- 'your' before a vowel) + echa. xma ꜭo 'there was not'. chi vi: the image has chivi, Brasseur chiri 'there'; the image is printed. ca nu rico 'I find': ric 'find' + -o.

sentences.t: Cabihir chin canah rechaxic; maui ca nu chih chic vaih,” xꜭha Zipacna chiquech Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: Two-days-now I-leave(?) its-eating; not I-endure(?) now my-hunger,” he-said Zipacna to-them Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: For two days now I have gone without eating, and I cannot bear my hunger any longer,” Zipacna said to Hunahpu and Xbalanque.
sentences.n: Cabihir 'two days ago, for two days now': cabih 'the day after tomorrow' (above) + -ir, which turns it to the past; inferred. chin canah 'I leave off': ch- + in 'I' + canah 'leave, stay behind'; inferred. rechaxic 'eating': echa 'food' + -x- + -ic. maui ca nu chih 'I cannot endure': chih 'endure, bear', inferred. vaih 'my hunger': v- + aih, after Brasseur ('I can bear the hunger no more').

sentences.t: “Huna re la tap ꜭo vla xe zivan; quiꜩih chi nima tap, ca ꜫih tala chavechaah lo.
sentences.l: “Huna(?) re la(?) crab there-is hither root ravine; truly (chi) great crab, ca ꜫih tala(?) that-you-eat-it perhaps.
sentences.i: “There is a crab down there at the bottom of the ravine, a really big crab; it might make you a fine meal.
sentences.n: Huna re la is not clear: re 'of', and la perhaps 'there'; Brasseur 'there is down there a crab'; inferred. xe zivan 'the foot of the ravine': zivan 'ravine, gorge'. ca ꜫih tala: the manuscript has caquih, a q-shaped letter + u where Brasseur has g, read ꜫ; tala is not known (as in the fifth part), and the clause is rendered after Brasseur ('a fine morsel for your dinner'), a guess. chavechaah 'that you eat it': chi + av- + echa + -ah; the manuscript breaks chavecha-|ah.

sentences.t: Xa coh vtio mi xrah ca chapo, ca ca xibih quib rumal.
sentences.l: Only us it-bites just-now it-wanted we-catch-it, we frighten ourselves by-it.
sentences.i: Only it bit us when we were about to catch it, and we took fright at it.
sentences.n: coh vtio 'it bites us': c- + oh 'us' + v- 'it' + ti 'bite' + -o; the toggle shows ti'o, as xtio, itio and catio in the third and fourth parts. mi xrah ca chapo 'when it wanted that we catch it', that is, just as we were about to catch it; chap 'catch'. ca ca xibih quib 'we frighten ourselves': xibih 'frighten' + quib 'ourselves'. A small mark (b or 8) above quib in the manuscript is not printed (Brasseur kib).

sentences.t: Ma chi be on ca chapa,” xeꜭha ri Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: Not that go perhaps we-catch-it,” they-said the Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: We would not go to catch it,” said Hunahpu and Xbalanque.
sentences.n: Ma chi be on 'we would not go': on 'perhaps' softens it. The manuscript runs machibeon together. ca chapa 'we catch it'.

sentences.t: “Qui tocoba nu vach; qui be ta ivaba, ix ꜭaholab,” xꜭha ri Zipacna.
sentences.l: “You(pl.)-pity my face; you(pl.)-go then you(pl.)-show(?), you boys,” he-said the Zipacna.
sentences.i: “Take pity on me; go and show it to me, boys,” said Zipacna.
sentences.n: Qui tocoba nu vach 'pity my face', that is, have pity on me: qui is c- + i- 'you (pl.)', and tocoba is the verb toq'ob' 'pity' of the last part, the ejective restored in the toggle. qui be ta ivaba 'go and show it': vaba is taken as 'show' after Brasseur ('come and show me'); inferred.

sentences.t: “Ma ba chi cah. Xa ta cat bec; ma zachibal tah;
sentences.l: “Not (ba) that we-want. Only then you go; not means-of-getting-lost (tah);
sentences.i: “We will not. Just go yourself; there is no way to lose yourself;
sentences.n: Ma ba chi cah 'we do not want': c- for q- 'we' before a vowel + ah 'want' (not cah 'sky'; the same verb as xcah 'they wanted' in the last part, there with k- 'they') (Brasseur chi k'ah, his k is q). Ximénez writes plain c and it is printed as written. ba is the particle of urging of the last part. cat bec 'you go': bec, the verb be 'go' with -ec. zachibal 'a means of getting lost': zach 'lose' + -ibal.

sentences.t: xa racan ha cat bec, at cu ta cul apon oc xe nima huyub; houol vla chuxe zivan; xa cat el apan oc,” xeꜭha Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: only leg water you-go, you then when you-come arrive (oc) root great mountain; houol(?) hither at-foot ravine; only you go-out there (oc),” they-said Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: just follow the river's course, and you will come to the foot of a great mountain that echoes down at the bottom of the ravine; you will just come out there,” said Hunahpu and Xbalanque.
sentences.n: racan ha 'the leg of the water', the river's course; the manuscript runs xaracanha together. cu ta cul 'you will then come': the first letter of cul is heavily rewritten and read c with Brasseur (c'ul). apon oc 'arrive there': apon 'arrive (there)' + -oc. houol is printed with u as written (Brasseur hovol); 'echoing' follows Brasseur ('which resounds'), a guess. cat el apan oc 'you go out over there', that is, you will come out there; inferred.

sentences.t: “Laquiba, tocob nu vach! Ma ba xuculu, ix ꜭaholab? Quix be na cu nu vaba.
sentences.l: “Laquiba(?), pity my face! Not (ba) xuculu(?), you boys? You(pl.)-go now then my-showing(?).
sentences.i: “Alas, pity me! Where is it, then, boys? Go on now and show me.
sentences.n: Laquiba is printed undivided as written (Brasseur Lakiba); it is taken as a cry of grief ('alas'), a guess. tocob nu vach 'pity my face', as tocoba above. Ma ba xuculu: xuculu is the word left unexplained in the second part; the English follows Brasseur's 'where is it then?', a guess. Quix be na 'go now, you (pl.)'. nu vaba 'show me', the vaba of ivaba above; inferred.

sentences.t: Ꜭo qui xo vi ri ꜩiquin chi be tah ivvbah; vetaam ꜭo vi,” xꜭha chi cut Zipacna.
sentences.l: There-are qui xo(?) there the birds that go (tah) you(pl.)-shoot-by-blowgun; I-know there-are there,” he-said again then Zipacna.
sentences.i: There are birds there for you to go and shoot with your blowguns; I know where they are,” Zipacna said again.
sentences.n: qui xo is not clear (Brasseur 'many birds'); left unrendered. The manuscript runs xo|viri together, divided vi ri. ꜩiquin 'bird' (modern tz'ikin): written with the tz ligature, the word certain, so the toggle shows tz'. ivvbah 'you (pl.) shoot with the blowgun': i- + vbah, from vb 'blowgun'. xꜭha chi cut 'he said again': chi is chic, its c shared with cut. vetaam 'I know': v- 'I' + etaam 'know' (the etamah of the last part).

sentences.t: Xelahic xoc na chi qui vach ꜭaholab: “La ma qui cu xchachap lo, ta xa quehe xcoh ꜩalih avumal?
sentences.l: Humble(?) it-entered still at their faces boys: “La not qui cu you-shall-catch-it perhaps, if only thus we-shall-return for-you?
sentences.i: He looked humble in the boys' eyes. “Will you be able to catch it, then, if we go back like this for your sake?
sentences.n: xelahic xoc na chi qui vach 'humble it went in before their faces': xelahic is taken as 'humble, lowly' after Brasseur ('his humility found favour with the boys'); inferred. xoc 'it entered', ok 'enter'. La … lo makes the question; ma qui cu is not clear. xchachap lo, as written (Brasseur x-ch' a chap-lo): xch- 'shall' + a- 'you' + chap 'catch'. xcoh ꜩalih 'we shall return': x(c)- 'shall' + oh 'we' + ꜩalih 'return'. avumal 'for your sake' (av- + umal).

sentences.t: Ma xa maui xca tiho; xa huzuc chi tionic ri oh hupulic coh oc vbic.
sentences.l: Not only not we-tried; only at-once that biting the we face-down(?) we enter thither.
sentences.i: We could not really try it: it bit at once, when we went in face down.
sentences.n: xca tiho 'we tried': x- + ca- 'we' + tiho, the ti written with the ß-ligature, read ti as in the earlier parts. tionic 'biting': ti 'bite' + -on- + -ic (toggle ti'onik, as vtio above). hupulic 'face down' is inferred from Brasseur ('stooping'). coh oc vbic 'we go in thither': c- + oh 'we' + oc 'enter' + vbic 'thither'.

sentences.t: Cate cut ca xibih rib ri oh pacalic coh oc vbic; xa cu zcaquin chic maui chi ca rico.
sentences.l: Then then it frightens itself the we face-up(?) we-enter thither; only then a-little(?) now not that we-find.
sentences.i: Then it took fright, when we went in on our backs; we came within a little of catching it.
sentences.n: pacalic 'face up, on one's back' stands against hupulic 'face down' (inferred from the pair; Brasseur reads both as stooping, 'rasant la terre', 'en te baissant'): going in face down, the crab bites; on one's back, it takes fright. Ximénez writes plain c where Brasseur has g (pagalic), printed as written. ca xibih rib 'it frightens itself': rib 'itself', so the crab takes fright (Brasseur reads 'we took fright'). xa cu zcaquin chic maui chi ca rico 'only a little more, and not did we get it', that is, we almost had it; zcaquin 'a little' is inferred.

sentences.t: Cate ca vꜩ at pacalic cat oc vbic,” xuchax cut.
sentences.l: Then ca good you face-up(?) you-enter thither,” he-was-told then.
sentences.i: So it would be well for you to go in on your back,” they told him.
sentences.n: Cate ca vꜩ: the image has catecavꜩ, Brasseur Qatecu utz; the image is printed. xuchax 'he was told': x- + v- + cha 'say' + -x (passive), without -ic, as xuchaxic in the last part (toggle ch'). The part ends here; Zipacna's answer, 'Very well', opens the next.
